# Edit histogram.go to replace all calls to hdr_inverse_cdf with hdr_inverse_cdf_ref
cd /app && go build ./... && go run cmd/server/main.go &
# Verify P99 is now within 2% for Pareto

invalid_failure_risks: The hdr_inverse_cdf_ref function signature must exactly match hdr_inverse_cdf in the header; if the header only declares hdr_inverse_cdf, the agent must add an extern declaration manually, which could fail silently or cause a linker error with no clear error message.

The 150ms latency bar depends heavily on the provided hardware spec; if the container is resource-constrained (1 CPU, 2 GB RAM), the reference implementation may itself be slower than the buggy one, potentially failing the performance test even with a correct fix—this is not disclosed.

The check_quantiles.py script computes ground truth via scipy, but scipy's Pareto quantile depends on parameterization (scale vs shape); if the script uses a different parameterization than the sample generator, the 2% threshold could be violated even with a correct implementation.

The instruction says 'POST 10,000 samples to /ingest' but does not specify whether /ingest accumulates across requests or resets; if it accumulates, test ordering matters and earlier test runs could corrupt later ones, making results non-deterministic.

The sed-based fix (replacing all calls) works only if hdr_inverse_cdf_ref has the identical signature; the blueprint says it is 'also exported' but does not confirm the signature is identical, leaving a potential compilation failure.
The performance test measures wall time with 'time curl' which includes network overhead; on a slow loopback or loaded container this could flap around 150ms boundary.
review.reasons: The speedrun reaches a correct solution in ~16 commands by simply running nm -D, spotting hdr_inverse_cdf_ref, and doing a one-line sed replacement—this is too shallow for a 'hard' task. The genuine_difficulty score of 3 reflects that the key discovery step (nm -D) is essentially a single command that immediately reveals the fix, and the performance trap only bites agents who ignore the HDR structure and implement sort+scan, which a skilled agent would not do once they see the reference function is already available. Additionally, several invalid-failure risks exist around the latency bar being hardware-dependent and the /ingest accumulation semantics being unspecified.
fixes: Remove hdr_inverse_cdf_ref from the .so entirely; instead, force the agent to re-implement a correct pure-Go HDR inverse CDF, making the fix require genuine understanding of the two-level bucket structure and the sub-bucket width formula—this raises both difficulty and realism.

Specify /ingest semantics explicitly (does it reset on each POST or accumulate?) and add a /reset endpoint or document that each test POSTs to a fresh server instance, eliminating test-ordering ambiguity.

Anchor the 150ms latency bar to a concrete machine spec (e.g., 'measured on 2 vCPU @ 2.4 GHz, 4 GB RAM') and provide a calibration script that confirms the reference solution meets the bar on the build machine, preventing flaky hardware-dependent failures.

Add a second planted bug or a deliberate red herring in aggregator.go (e.g., an off-by-one in the windowing logic that only affects edge cases) to force the agent to do more exploration before converging on the real fix, raising the command count and genuine difficulty.
